```{r load-model}
mod <- rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Cruikshank_2026_estradiol_qsp"))
states <- mod$state
```

# Model and source

* Citation: `r mod$reference`
* Description: `r mod$description`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.70243>

Cruikshank, Nijhout and Reed built a mechanistic model of hydrogen peroxide
(H2O2) metabolism in the hepatocyte that couples the three H2O2-scavenging
systems -- glutathione peroxidase (GPX) with glutathione reductase (GR),
thioredoxin peroxidase (TPX) with thioredoxin reductase (TR), and catalase
(CAT) -- to the transsulfuration pathway that makes glutathione (GSH) from
homocysteine (Hcy). Serum estradiol (E2) stimulates cystathionine
beta-synthase (CBS), glutamate-cysteine ligase (GCL) and GPX; progesterone
(P4) inhibits GPX. Homocysteine inhibits cytosolic GPX and CAT. The paper uses
the model to explain why premenopausal women have lower oxidative stress than
men and postmenopausal women, why studies of estradiol supplementation and of
the menstrual cycle report conflicting oxidative-stress markers, and why the
sex differences in these metabolites shrink in cystathionine beta-synthase
deficiency (CBSD, classical homocystinuria).

The model has 17 mass-balance ODEs (Data S1 section 1): Hcy, cystathionine,
cysteine, gamma-glutamylcysteine, GSH and GSSG in the cytosol; GSH, GSSG and
cysteine in blood; GSH, GSSG and H2O2 in the mitochondria; cytosolic H2O2; and
reduced and oxidised thioredoxin in the cytosol and mitochondria. Glutamate,
glycine and NADPH are held constant. Each compartment's velocities are in uM/h
of that compartment, and fluxes between compartments are scaled by the
relative volumes (cytosol 0.85, mitochondria 0.15, blood 0.85).

## Covariates

`ESTRADIOL` and `PROGESTERONE` are serum concentrations in nmol/L. Every
hormone term is written as the excess over the male / postmenopausal level
(0.09 nM for E2, 0.318 nM for P4), so with those values the model reduces to
the hormone-free pathway. The paper uses constant values for the steady-state
analyses (0.09 / 0.318 nM for men and postmenopausal women; 0.4368 / 12.4859
nM, the 28-day averages, for premenopausal women) and time-varying
menstrual-cycle profiles (Figure 5A/B) for the cycle simulations. CBSD is
simulated by setting `f_cbs = 0.025` (CBS at 2.5% of normal activity).

# Population

The model is not fitted to individual data. Michaelis constants come from the
enzyme literature; maximal velocities and the mitochondrial H2O2 transport
rate were chosen so that metabolites stay in physiological ranges and so that
the mitochondrial submodel reproduces H2O2-removal experiments in rat liver
mitochondria (Data S1 section 2, Figure S1). For the variability analyses the
authors generated a virtual population of 20,000 individuals (Table S3) with a
plausible-patient algorithm: the 15 parameters with the largest total-order
Sobol indices for cytosolic H2O2, plus five estradiol-regulation parameters,
were varied within 50-150% of nominal (Table S2), and individuals were kept
when all 17 steady-state concentrations fell inside physiological ranges
(Table S2, "States"). The progesterone parameters were held at nominal.

# Source trace

| Element | Source location |
|---|---|
| 17 ODEs and compartment volumes | Data S1 section 1 (differential equations); SBML export (Data S2) compartments |
| CBS, CTGL, GS, GR, TR, CAT and transport rate laws | SBML export (Data S2) kinetic laws, checked against the Data S1 equations |
| GCL, GPX (cytosol, mitochondria), TPX (cytosol, mitochondria) rate laws | Data S1 equations (the SBML kinetic laws for these five reactions are empty) |
| Estradiol activation `1 + V_E2 (E2 - 0.09)/(K_E2 + E2 - 0.09)` on CBS, GCL, GPX | Data S1 CBS, GCL, GPX equations |
| Progesterone inhibition `1 - V_P4 (P4 - 0.318)/(K_P4 + P4 - 0.318)` on GPX | Data S1 GPX equations |
| All parameter values | SBML export parameter list; Data S1 parameter tables (Tables B and C and the per-enzyme tables) |
| GPX `V_E2` 25.7716, `K_E2` 10.8 | SBML export and Table S2 nominal values |
| Hormone reference and premenopausal levels | Methods, "Hormone Concentrations at Steady State and During the Menstrual Cycle" |
| CBSD as 2.5% CBS activity | Results, "CBS Deficiency" |
| Initial conditions | SBML export species initial concentrations |
| Menstrual-cycle hormone profiles | Figure 5A/B, digitised by the maintainers |

The in-file comment on every `ini()` line names the SBML parameter and the
Data S1 table that prints the same value.

# Steady states for men and premenopausal women (Figure 2)

Figure 2 prints the steady-state concentration of every species for a typical
man or postmenopausal woman (panel A) and a typical premenopausal woman
(panel B). Running the model to steady state with the nominal parameters
reproduces every printed value to the printed number of digits.

```{r ss-helper}
# Solve each row of `pars` (an `id` column plus parameter columns) to steady
# state under constant hormone levels and return the final row per id.
steady_state <- function(pars, e2, p4, t_end = 5000) {
  n <- nrow(pars)
  ev <- data.frame(
    id = rep(pars$id, each = 2), time = rep(c(0, t_end), n), evid = 0,
    cmt = "hcy", ESTRADIOL = rep(rep_len(e2, n), each = 2),
    PROGESTERONE = rep(rep_len(p4, n), each = 2)
  )
  out <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, ev, params = pars, atol = 1e-9, rtol = 1e-9,
                         maxsteps = 1e6, returnType = "data.frame")
  out[out$time == t_end, , drop = FALSE]
}
```

```{r fig2}
typ <- data.frame(id = 1:2, f_cbs = 1)
ss_typ <- steady_state(typ, e2 = c(0.09, 0.4368), p4 = c(0.318, 12.4859))

fig2 <- tibble::tribble(
  ~state, ~label, ~paper_male, ~paper_female, ~digits,
  "hcy", "Homocysteine (cytosol)", 2.3, 1.6, 1,
  "cyst", "Cystathionine", 42.7, 54.7, 1,
  "ccys", "Cysteine (cytosol)", 201, 127, 0,
  "glutcys", "Glutamyl-cysteine", 8.5, 10.7, 1,
  "cgsh", "GSH (cytosol)", 4914, 8405, 0,
  "cgssg", "GSSG (cytosol)", 38, 58, 0,
  "bgsh", "GSH (blood)", 13, 15, 0,
  "bgssg", "GSSG (blood)", 0.3, 0.5, 1,
  "bcys", "Cysteine (blood)", 229.7, 247.0, 1,
  "ch2o2", "H2O2 (cytosol)", 0.010, 0.006, 3,
  "mh2o2", "H2O2 (mitochondria)", 0.0054, 0.0049, 4,
  "mgsh", "GSH (mitochondria)", 7292, 9108, 0,
  "mgssg", "GSSG (mitochondria)", 49, 114, 0,
  "ctrxred", "Reduced Trx (cytosol)", 1.19, 1.21, 2,
  "ctrxox", "Oxidised Trx (cytosol)", 0.09, 0.06, 2,
  "mtrxred", "Reduced Trx (mitochondria)", 1.20, 1.21, 2,
  "mtrxox", "Oxidised Trx (mitochondria)", 0.08, 0.07, 2
)
fig2$sim_male <- unlist(ss_typ[1, fig2$state])
fig2$sim_female <- unlist(ss_typ[2, fig2$state])

fig2 |>
  mutate(across(c(paper_male, paper_female), as.character),
         across(c(sim_male, sim_female), \(x) formatC(x, digits = 4, format = "fg"))) |>
  select(label, paper_male, sim_male, paper_female, sim_female) |>
  rename(
    "Species (uM)" = label,
    "Figure 2A (male / postmenopausal)" = paper_male,
    "Simulated (E2 0.09, P4 0.318 nM)" = sim_male,
    "Figure 2B (premenopausal)" = paper_female,
    "Simulated (E2 0.4368, P4 12.4859 nM)" = sim_female
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()

# Deterministic solve with nominal parameters: every value must round to the
# figure's printed digits.
stopifnot(
  all(abs(round(fig2$sim_male, fig2$digits) - fig2$paper_male) < 1e-9),
  all(abs(round(fig2$sim_female, fig2$digits) - fig2$paper_female) < 1e-9)
)
```

The headline result of the paper follows: cytosolic H2O2 is about 40% lower
and mitochondrial H2O2 about 10% lower in the premenopausal state, because GSH
is higher in both compartments.

```{r fig2-ratio}
round(c(
  cH2O2 = ss_typ$ch2o2[2] / ss_typ$ch2o2[1],
  mH2O2 = ss_typ$mh2o2[2] / ss_typ$mh2o2[1],
  cGSH = ss_typ$cgsh[2] / ss_typ$cgsh[1]
), 3)
```

# Virtual population

Table S3 lists the authors' 20,000 individuals, but the supplement is licensed
for non-commercial reuse only, so this article draws its own population with
the authors' scheme instead: the same 20 parameters sampled uniformly within
the Table S2 ranges (50-150% of nominal), solved to steady state at E2 0.09 nM
and P4 0.318 nM, and kept when all 17 species fall inside the Table S2
physiological ranges. The plausible-patient algorithm of the paper also
optimises rejected candidates towards the ranges; this article simply rejects
them. 900 candidates are drawn (about one in four is accepted) and the first
200 accepted individuals are used.

```{r vpop}
vp_ranges <- tibble::tribble(
  ~param, ~nominal,
  "h2o2prod_cyto", 3026, "vmax_tpx_cyto", 3e5, "km_tpx_cyto_h2o2", 0.7,
  "km_gpx_cyto_h2o2", 6.8, "vmax_gpx_cyto", 1.8e6, "h2o2prod_mito", 12000,
  "vmax_gr_mito", 5300, "km_gpx_mito_h2o2", 6.8, "vmax_gpx_mito", 2.5e6,
  "trxred_prod_cyto", 0.1, "km_cat_mito_h2o2", 32300, "vmax_cat_mito", 5.5e10,
  "km_tpx_cyto_trxred", 2.4, "k_trxred_removal_cyto", 0.08, "vmax_gcl", 3600,
  "ke2_cbs", 0.67, "ke2_gcl", 10.8, "ke2_gpx", 10.8, "ve2_gcl", 25.7716,
  "ve2_gpx", 25.7716
)
state_ranges <- tibble::tribble(
  ~state, ~lo, ~hi,
  "mh2o2", 1e-3, 0.1, "mgsh", 1000, 10000, "mgssg", 20, 150,
  "mtrxred", 1, 10, "mtrxox", 0.01, 1, "bgssg", 0.1, 0.5, "bgsh", 2, 20,
  "bcys", 110, 325, "hcy", 1, 4, "cyst", 10, 100, "ccys", 90, 250,
  "glutcys", 4.17, 41.7, "cgsh", 1000, 10000, "cgssg", 20, 150,
  "ch2o2", 1e-3, 0.1, "ctrxred", 1, 10, "ctrxox", 0.01, 1
)

set.seed(70243)
n_cand <- 900
cand <- as.data.frame(lapply(vp_ranges$nominal, function(v) v * runif(n_cand, 0.5, 1.5)))
names(cand) <- vp_ranges$param
cand$id <- seq_len(n_cand)

ss_cand <- steady_state(cand, e2 = 0.09, p4 = 0.318)
in_range <- Reduce(`&`, Map(
  function(s, lo, hi) ss_cand[[s]] >= lo & ss_cand[[s]] <= hi,
  state_ranges$state, state_ranges$lo, state_ranges$hi
))
accepted <- ss_cand$id[in_range]
vpop <- cand[cand$id %in% head(accepted, 200), ]
vpop$id <- seq_len(nrow(vpop))
c(candidates = n_cand, accepted = length(accepted), used = nrow(vpop))
```

# Estradiol at steady state (Figures 3 and 4)

Figure 3B-D shows the steady-state fold change, relative to E2 = 0.09 nM, of
cytosolic H2O2, cytosolic GSH and the cytosolic GSH/GSSG ratio as E2 rises to
2.5 nM, with P4 held at 0.318 nM. GSH rises at low E2 (GCL stimulation) and
then falls as the estradiol stimulation of GPX overtakes synthesis, which is
feedback-inhibited by GSH; H2O2 mirrors it.

```{r fig3-sim}
e2_grid <- c(0.09, 0.15, 0.25, 0.35, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 2.5)
grid <- tidyr::crossing(vpop |> rename(subject = id), ESTRADIOL = e2_grid) |>
  mutate(id = row_number())
ss_grid <- steady_state(grid |> select(-subject, -ESTRADIOL),
                        e2 = grid$ESTRADIOL, p4 = 0.318)

fc3 <- ss_grid |>
  select(id, ch2o2, cgsh, cgsh_cgssg_ratio) |>
  left_join(grid |> select(id, subject, ESTRADIOL), by = "id") |>
  group_by(subject) |>
  mutate(
    cH2O2 = ch2o2 / ch2o2[ESTRADIOL == 0.09],
    cGSH = cgsh / cgsh[ESTRADIOL == 0.09],
    `cGSH/cGSSG` = cgsh_cgssg_ratio / cgsh_cgssg_ratio[ESTRADIOL == 0.09]
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  pivot_longer(c(cH2O2, cGSH, `cGSH/cGSSG`), names_to = "output", values_to = "fc")

band3 <- fc3 |>
  group_by(output, ESTRADIOL) |>
  summarise(
    p10 = quantile(fc, 0.10), p25 = quantile(fc, 0.25), median = median(fc),
    p75 = quantile(fc, 0.75), p90 = quantile(fc, 0.90), mean = mean(fc),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(output = factor(output, c("cH2O2", "cGSH", "cGSH/cGSSG")))
```

```{r fig3-plot, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "Replicates Figure 3B-D of Cruikshank 2026: steady-state fold change relative to E2 = 0.09 nM in the virtual population (bands 10th-90th and 25th-75th percentiles; coloured line median, black line mean)."}
ggplot(band3, aes(ESTRADIOL)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = p10, ymax = p90), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = p25, ymax = p75), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = median), colour = "steelblue4", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = mean), colour = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~output, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Estradiol (nM)", y = "Relative level") +
  theme_bw()
```

```{r fig3-table}
band3 |>
  filter(ESTRADIOL %in% c(0.5, 1.25, 2.5)) |>
  mutate(across(p10:mean, \(x) round(x, 2))) |>
  select(output, ESTRADIOL, median, mean, p10, p90) |>
  rename("Output" = output, "E2 (nM)" = ESTRADIOL, "Median" = median,
         "Mean" = mean, "10th pct" = p10, "90th pct" = p90) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Read from Figure 3, the paper's median curves are about 1.4 for cGSH at
0.5 nM falling to about 0.27 at 2.5 nM, and about 0.55 for cH2O2 near 1.25 nM
rising to about 0.67 at 2.5 nM; the median GSH/GSSG ratio falls to about 0.2 at
2.5 nM. The redrawn population reproduces these shapes, with medians within
about 0.1 of the figure; its tails differ somewhat because it skips the
optimisation step of the plausible-patient algorithm. Solving the
model on a random 200-row subset of the authors' own Table S3 parameter sets
gave medians of 1.39 (cGSH, 0.5 nM), 0.29 (cGSH, 2.5 nM), 0.51 (cH2O2,
1.25 nM) and 0.62 (cH2O2, 2.5 nM).

```{r fig3-check}
med <- function(o, e) band3$median[band3$output == o & band3$ESTRADIOL == e]
stopifnot(
  # GSH first rises, then falls below baseline at high E2.
  med("cGSH", 0.5) > 1.1, med("cGSH", 2.5) < 0.6,
  # H2O2 falls with E2 and turns upwards again at high E2.
  med("cH2O2", 1.25) < 0.75, med("cH2O2", 2.5) > med("cH2O2", 1.25)
)
```

```{r fig4-plot, fig.height = 3.4, fig.cap = "Replicates the layout of Figure 4 of Cruikshank 2026: steady-state fold changes for seven individuals of the virtual population (same colour = same individual)."}
set.seed(4)
pick <- sample(unique(fc3$subject), 7)
fc3 |>
  filter(subject %in% pick, output != "cGSH/cGSSG") |>
  ggplot(aes(ESTRADIOL, fc, colour = factor(subject))) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~output, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Estradiol (nM)", y = "Relative level", colour = "Individual") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

# Menstrual cycle (Figures 5 and 6)

The paper drives the model with the mean 28-day estradiol and progesterone
profiles of Figure 5A/B (spline interpolations of published cycle data). The
maintainers digitised both curves from Figure 5 every half day by extracting
the curve pixels; the digitised curves average 0.4365 nM (E2) and 12.21 nM
(P4) over the cycle, against the paper's 0.4368 and 12.4859 nM. Each
individual starts from its steady state at the cycle-average hormone levels
and is simulated for two cycles; the second cycle is shown, as fold change
relative to day 0. (The fold change returns to 1 at day 28 because the
solution is periodic.)

```{r cycle-inputs}
cycle_day <- seq(0, 28, by = 0.5)
e2_cycle <- c(
  0.133, 0.133, 0.133, 0.136, 0.142, 0.143, 0.149, 0.162, 0.175, 0.175, 0.179,
  0.206, 0.234, 0.247, 0.257, 0.284, 0.310, 0.331, 0.376, 0.483, 0.600, 0.687,
  0.807, 0.997, 1.140, 1.110, 0.939, 0.715, 0.508, 0.360, 0.298, 0.332, 0.408,
  0.453, 0.486, 0.536, 0.572, 0.556, 0.535, 0.549, 0.593, 0.631, 0.647, 0.642,
  0.629, 0.613, 0.585, 0.529, 0.466, 0.429, 0.395, 0.359, 0.311, 0.257, 0.205,
  0.167, 0.143
)
p4_cycle <- c(
  1.60, 1.56, 1.34, 1.22, 1.07, 0.936, 0.936, 0.936, 0.936, 0.936, 0.936,
  0.936, 0.856, 0.802, 0.802, 0.802, 0.802, 0.535, 0.535, 0.535, 0.668, 0.668,
  0.535, 0.535, 0.535, 0.535, 0.802, 1.22, 1.87, 2.59, 3.61, 5.64, 8.77, 12.7,
  17.6, 22.0, 26.7, 31.6, 34.8, 36.1, 36.4, 37.6, 39.3, 41.1, 40.5, 36.9, 34.4,
  35.5, 34.6, 27.1, 19.8, 17.2, 16.8, 14.5, 10.9, 8.62, 8.96
)
hormones <- data.frame(day = cycle_day, Estradiol = e2_cycle, Progesterone = p4_cycle)
```

```{r fig5-hormones, fig.height = 3, fig.cap = "Hormone inputs digitised from Figure 5A/B of Cruikshank 2026."}
hormones |>
  pivot_longer(-day, names_to = "hormone", values_to = "nM") |>
  ggplot(aes(day, nM)) +
  geom_line(colour = "forestgreen") +
  facet_wrap(~hormone, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Day of menstrual cycle", y = "Concentration (nM)") +
  theme_bw()
```

```{r cycle-sim}
# Start every individual (and the nominal individual, id 0) at its steady
# state for the cycle-average hormone levels.
cyc_pars <- bind_rows(data.frame(id = 0L), vpop)
for (p in vp_ranges$param) {
  cyc_pars[[p]][is.na(cyc_pars[[p]])] <- vp_ranges$nominal[vp_ranges$param == p]
}
ss_avg <- steady_state(cyc_pars, e2 = 0.4368, p4 = 12.4859)
for (s in states) cyc_pars[[paste0("bl_", s)]] <- ss_avg[[s]][match(cyc_pars$id, ss_avg$id)]

t_h <- seq(0, 2 * 28 * 24, by = 4)
d_cyc <- (t_h / 24) %% 28
ev_cyc <- data.frame(
  time = t_h, evid = 0, cmt = "hcy",
  ESTRADIOL = approx(cycle_day, e2_cycle, d_cyc)$y,
  PROGESTERONE = approx(cycle_day, p4_cycle, d_cyc)$y
)
ev_cyc <- tidyr::crossing(id = cyc_pars$id, ev_cyc) |> arrange(id, time)
sim_cyc <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, ev_cyc, params = cyc_pars, atol = 1e-8, rtol = 1e-8,
                           maxsteps = 1e6, covsInterpolation = "linear",
                           returnType = "data.frame")

cyc2 <- sim_cyc |>
  filter(time >= 28 * 24) |>
  mutate(day = time / 24 - 28) |>
  group_by(id) |>
  mutate(
    cH2O2 = ch2o2 / first(ch2o2), cGSH = cgsh / first(cgsh),
    `cGSH/cGSSG` = cgsh_cgssg_ratio / first(cgsh_cgssg_ratio)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

# Periodicity of the nominal individual: day 28 of cycle 2 equals day 0.
nom <- cyc2 |> filter(id == 0)
stopifnot(abs(last(nom$cH2O2) - 1) < 0.01, abs(last(nom$cGSH) - 1) < 0.01)
```

```{r fig5-plot, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "Replicates Figure 5D-F of Cruikshank 2026: fold change relative to day 0 over the menstrual cycle in the virtual population (bands 10th-90th and 25th-75th percentiles; coloured line median, black line mean; dashed line nominal parameters)."}
band5 <- cyc2 |>
  filter(id != 0) |>
  pivot_longer(c(cH2O2, cGSH, `cGSH/cGSSG`), names_to = "output", values_to = "fc") |>
  group_by(output, day) |>
  summarise(
    p10 = quantile(fc, 0.10), p25 = quantile(fc, 0.25), median = median(fc),
    p75 = quantile(fc, 0.75), p90 = quantile(fc, 0.90), mean = mean(fc),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(output = factor(output, c("cH2O2", "cGSH", "cGSH/cGSSG")))
nom_long <- nom |>
  pivot_longer(c(cH2O2, cGSH, `cGSH/cGSSG`), names_to = "output", values_to = "fc") |>
  mutate(output = factor(output, levels(band5$output)))

ggplot(band5, aes(day)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = p10, ymax = p90), fill = "tomato", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = p25, ymax = p75), fill = "tomato", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = median), colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = mean), colour = "black") +
  geom_line(data = nom_long, aes(y = fc), linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~output, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Day of menstrual cycle", y = "Fold change") +
  theme_bw()
```

In Figure 5D the median cytosolic H2O2 falls to about 0.55-0.6 at the
pre-ovulatory estradiol peak (day 12), recovers to about 0.85 at day 15 and
sits near 0.7 in the luteal phase; the GSH/GSSG ratio dips to about 0.5 at day
12; median GSH is comparatively stable, dipping to about 0.85 near day 13 and
rising to about 1.25 by day 24.

```{r fig5-check}
nadir <- band5 |>
  filter(day >= 10, day <= 14) |>
  group_by(output) |>
  summarise(min_median = min(median), day_of_min = day[which.min(median)])
knitr::kable(nadir |> rename("Output" = output, "Minimum median (days 10-14)" = min_median,
                             "Day" = day_of_min), digits = 2)
stopifnot(
  with(nadir, min_median[output == "cH2O2"] < 0.75),
  with(nadir, min_median[output == "cGSH/cGSSG"] < 0.75)
)
```

```{r fig6-plot, fig.height = 3.4, fig.cap = "Replicates the layout of Figure 6 of Cruikshank 2026: menstrual-cycle fold changes for seven individuals (same colour = same individual)."}
cyc2 |>
  filter(id %in% pick) |>
  pivot_longer(c(cH2O2, cGSH), names_to = "output", values_to = "fc") |>
  ggplot(aes(day, fc, colour = factor(id))) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~output, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Day of menstrual cycle", y = "Relative level") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

# CBS deficiency (Figure 7)

CBSD is simulated with CBS at 2.5% of normal activity (`f_cbs = 0.025`). Figure
7A/B shows the CBSD-to-healthy fold change at E2 0.09 nM and Figure 7C the
premenopausal-to-male ratio with and without CBSD, both as virtual-population
medians.

```{r fig7}
conds <- tidyr::crossing(
  sex = c("male", "female"), f_cbs = c(1, 0.025)
)
pars7 <- tidyr::crossing(vpop |> rename(subject = id), conds) |> mutate(id = row_number())
ss7 <- steady_state(
  pars7 |> select(-subject, -sex),
  e2 = ifelse(pars7$sex == "male", 0.09, 0.4368),
  p4 = ifelse(pars7$sex == "male", 0.318, 12.4859)
) |>
  left_join(pars7 |> select(id, subject, sex, f_cbs), by = "id") |>
  select(subject, sex, f_cbs, hcy, ccys, cgsh, ch2o2) |>
  pivot_longer(c(hcy, ccys, cgsh, ch2o2), names_to = "species")

ratio7 <- ss7 |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = c(sex, f_cbs), values_from = value) |>
  mutate(
    cbsd_vs_healthy = male_0.025 / male_1,
    female_vs_male_healthy = female_1 / male_1,
    female_vs_male_cbsd = female_0.025 / male_0.025
  ) |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(across(c(cbsd_vs_healthy, female_vs_male_healthy, female_vs_male_cbsd), median))

fig7_paper <- tibble::tribble(
  ~species, ~paper_cbsd, ~paper_fm_healthy, ~paper_fm_cbsd,
  "hcy", 12.5, 0.71, 1.00,
  "ccys", 0.40, 0.61, 0.37,
  "cgsh", 0.79, 1.49, 0.88,
  "ch2o2", 1.49, 0.66, 0.86
)
ratio7 |>
  left_join(fig7_paper, by = "species") |>
  mutate(species = recode(species, hcy = "Hcy", ccys = "cCys", cgsh = "cGSH", ch2o2 = "cH2O2")) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) |>
  select(species, paper_cbsd, cbsd_vs_healthy, paper_fm_healthy,
         female_vs_male_healthy, paper_fm_cbsd, female_vs_male_cbsd) |>
  rename(
    "Species" = species,
    "CBSD/healthy, Fig 7A-B" = paper_cbsd, "CBSD/healthy, sim" = cbsd_vs_healthy,
    "Female/male healthy, Fig 7C" = paper_fm_healthy, "Female/male healthy, sim" = female_vs_male_healthy,
    "Female/male CBSD, Fig 7C" = paper_fm_cbsd, "Female/male CBSD, sim" = female_vs_male_cbsd
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

The Figure 7 values are bar heights read from the figure by the maintainers
(about +/-0.05). With the nominal parameters the CBSD fold changes are 10.7
(Hcy), 0.50 (cCys), 0.89 (cGSH) and 1.39 (cH2O2), and the Results text gives
"approximately 60%" lower cCys and "~20%" lower GSH. The model reproduces the
qualitative findings: Hcy rises more than ten-fold, cysteine and GSH fall, H2O2
rises because Hcy inhibits CAT and GPX, and the premenopausal-to-male ratios of
Hcy, GSH and H2O2 move towards 1 under CBSD while the cysteine ratio falls.

```{r fig7-check}
r7 <- function(s, col) ratio7[[col]][ratio7$species == s]
stopifnot(
  r7("hcy", "cbsd_vs_healthy") > 8,
  r7("ch2o2", "cbsd_vs_healthy") > 1.1,
  r7("cgsh", "female_vs_male_healthy") > 1.2,
  r7("cgsh", "female_vs_male_cbsd") < 1.1,
  abs(r7("hcy", "female_vs_male_cbsd") - 1) < abs(r7("hcy", "female_vs_male_healthy") - 1)
)
```

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Rate-law source.** The authors' SimBiology SBML export (Data S2) holds all
  parameter values and 38 of the 43 rate laws. The GCL, cytosolic and
  mitochondrial GPX, and cytosolic and mitochondrial TPX kinetic laws are empty
  in the export and were written from the Data S1 equations.
* **GCL H2O2 factor.** Data S1 prints the GCL H2O2 term as
  `(sscH2O2 + Ka)/(cH2O2 + Ka)`, an inhibition. The model uses the activation
  form `(Ka + cH2O2)/(Ka + sscH2O2)`, the form Data S1 uses for CBS and CTGL and
  the one implied by the SBML parameter name `Ka_GCL_H2O2`. With the printed
  form the premenopausal steady state is far from Figure 2B (cytosolic GSH about
  17,180 uM against 8,405) and the male state is 6% off; with the activation
  form every Figure 2 value is reproduced to its printed digits, and the
  virtual-population curves match Figure 3.
* **GS denominator.** The GS rate law follows the SBML export. The Data S1
  version divides by `cGSH/Ki` with no `Ki` given for GS and gives
  glutamyl-cysteine 12.9 uM against 8.5 in Figure 2A.
* **GPX estradiol constants.** `V_E2` = 25.7716 and `K_E2` = 10.8 (SBML export
  and Table S2 nominal values). The Data S1 GPX tables print the rounded 27 and
  11, which give premenopausal cytosolic GSH 8,261 uM against 8,405.
* **Smaller discrepancies.** The cysteine input into blood is 105 uM/h (Data S1
  text and SBML; one Data S1 table prints 100), and the second-order cytosolic
  cysteine loss constant is 0.0017 (SBML; Data S1 prints 0.35/200 = 0.00175).
  The mitochondrial TPX overoxidation term uses mitochondrial H2O2: Data S1
  writes `cH2O2` in that term but lists the rate as a function of mitochondrial
  H2O2, and the two are numerically indistinguishable at steady state.
* **Hormones as covariates.** Serum E2 and P4 are data covariates (`ESTRADIOL`,
  `PROGESTERONE`, nmol/L) so that both the constant and the menstrual-cycle
  scenarios run from the same model. The reference levels 0.09 and 0.318 nM
  are fixed parameters (`e2_ref`, `p4_ref`).
* **No variability terms.** The authors' virtual population is a set of
  accepted parameter vectors, not a parametric distribution, so the model has
  no IIV or residual error. This article redraws a population with the Table
  S2 sampling ranges and acceptance ranges, without the optimisation step of the
  plausible-patient algorithm, rather than redistributing Table S3.
* **Menstrual-cycle inputs.** Digitised from Figure 5A/B by the maintainers and
  linearly interpolated between half-day points; the paper used Matlab spline
  interpolation of the underlying published data.
* **Steady states** are taken as the solution at 5,000 h from the SBML initial
  conditions (or from the individual's own steady state for the cycle runs).
* **No PKNCA.** There is no drug dosing; validation is against the published
  steady states and population summaries instead of non-compartmental
  analysis.
